text: I'll start by importing the STEP file and finding out what's actually in it.
The previous section drew all three solids in one colour and told me little. Re-emitting with the compound bound inside the cell and one colour per solid.

Measured facts about this file, all from the import:

- Declares **SI metre** (`LENGTH_UNIT + SI_UNIT($,.METRE.)`, no prefix); raw coordinates are ~0.027, so OCCT reads it as mm-numbers → real size **53.95 × 46.29 × 31.30 mm**.
- **3 solids**, named `LD19_BASE`, `LD19_EMITTER`, `LD19_BODY` (a LD19 lidar module), each a **single closed shell** (34/29/15 faces) — so no solid contains an internal cavity.
- Their volumes are 2552.3 + 12186.1 + 26455.7 mm³ and the fused union is **41193.9 mm³ exactly the sum** — the parts do not overlap and enclose nothing between them; they are stacked in contact (base plate z 0–1.5, body 1.5–20.1, emitter 20.1–31.3), with the body a near-full 38.5 mm block (26456 mm³ against a 27600 mm³ bbox) and the emitter a near-full cylinder.
- The only through-features are 3 small mounting holes in the base plate (3 inner wires on the z=0 face) and 3 standoff bosses outside the body footprint.

There is therefore no enclosed air space inside this assembly, no openings to cap, and nothing that can be called an inlet or an outlet. Producing a mesh would mean inventing an external wind-tunnel box whose every dimension, and whose inlet/outlet faces, came from me and not from the file or the request — which is redesigning, not preparing. I did not check for gaps below OCCT's 5e-6 m tolerance; if the intent was the sub-micron rotor clearance, that is not meshable at any sane cell size either.
